analysis.one_liner: Creates universal child care and early learning with family fees capped at 7% of income.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2019 and referred to the Senate health committee, the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a universal child care and early learning program for every child from six weeks old until the age when school attendance is required, regardless of income, disability, or citizenship status [S2][S3]. Families below twice the poverty line would pay nothing; everyone else would pay on a sliding scale capped at 7% of family income, no matter how many children they have enrolled [S2][S3]. The federal government would fund it through an open-ended, uncapped entitlement, with sponsors required to pay child care staff set compensation and to bargain with their unions [S3]. The bill was never taken up by the committee it was referred to [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children, especially low- and middle-income families who today pay some of the highest child care costs in the world; child care workers, who would get required minimum compensation and union bargaining rights; and local communities, which would run programs through states, cities, tribes, and nonprofits [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with young children and child care workers

how_it_helps.text: Every child from six weeks of age until compulsory school age would be entitled to a spot in the program, with no cap on the entitlement and no income test for eligibility [S3].

Families below 200% of the poverty line would pay no fee; above that, fees would rise on a sliding scale but never exceed 7% of family income, and the cap applies to the whole family no matter how many children are enrolled [S2][S3].
Services would be full-working-day (at least 10 hours) and full calendar year, including nonstandard-hours care for shift workers, with both center-based and home-based options [S3].
Sponsors would have to pay teachers and staff compensation meeting federal requirements and recognize and bargain with unions representing center staff and family child care home providers [S3].
The federal share would be 80% of costs for low-income children, 100% for children of migrant farmworkers and Native American children, and 50% for other children [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an open-ended appropriation ('such sums as may be necessary') that is not capped; higher-income families would pay up to 7% of income in fees, generally well below what full-price child care costs today [S3].

drawbacks.text: The core program is an uncapped entitlement — 'such sums as may be necessary' — so its total cost would be open-ended and very large, and the bill was estimated by outside analysts to cost on the order of hundreds of billions of dollars over a decade.

Because it is universal, substantial subsidies would also flow to higher-income families who could pay market rates, which raises the price tag without targeting the families most burdened by child care costs.

Requiring much higher staff pay and national standards would raise the cost of delivering care, and the bill's own mechanism — requiring sponsors to show the federal share is sufficient to meet compensation requirements — acknowledges those costs [S3].

Expanding demand for care faster than the supply of qualified workers and facilities could produce waiting lists or quality problems in the early years, particularly in rural areas and child care deserts.
Sponsors may delegate services to for-profit providers, so a share of the new federal spending would flow to private child care businesses, subject to the bill's standards and wage rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families with young children this would be one of the largest new social benefits since the creation of Head Start, directly replacing child care bills that for many families rival rent. The honest cost is real: an uncapped, universal entitlement is among the most expensive designs possible, and the same wage and quality requirements that help workers raise the price of delivery. A means-tested or capped version would cost less; the universal design buys political durability and simplicity at a very high price. On the merits, the benefits to working families and to child care workers are large and the bill takes the cost seriously enough to build wage sufficiency into its funding formula, but its open-ended funding makes the fiscal commitment enormous.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no action on it before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, so it died without a hearing, a vote, or ever reaching the Senate floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on June 18, 2019, joined by three Democratic cosponsors: Sens. Booker, Merkley, and Markey [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action of any kind appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].
The bill would have established an uncapped federal entitlement to child care for children from six weeks old, with fees waived below 200% of poverty and capped at 7% of family income [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, no family saw its child care costs fall and no worker saw the wage provisions take effect. The parties better off as things stand are the federal treasury, which avoided an open-ended spending commitment, and existing child care providers, which face no new federal wage mandates, union-bargaining obligations, or national standards.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury and incumbent child care providers

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Universal Child Care and Early Learning Act and recruited three Democratic cosponsors.

against.role: Committee of referral; took no action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two years after referral, leaving it to die in committee.

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All four Senate supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the Republican-chaired committee and Republican-run Senate majority let the bill sit without action until Congress expired.

industries.industry: Child care and early learning providers (centers and family child care homes)
industries.note: The bill would make existing and new providers the permanent delivery channel for a universal public benefit, routing federal money to them through prime and delegate provider agreements, including for-profit agencies. In exchange they would face national program standards, facility codes, required staff pay levels, and union recognition [S3].

industries.industry: Child care and early learning workers
industries.note: Sponsors must pay staff compensation meeting federal requirements and bargain with unions representing teachers, staff, and home-based providers — directly raising pay in one of the lowest-wage workforces in the country [S3].

For-profit agencies qualify as delegate providers and could receive federal program funds, but only under the bill's wage, union, and standards requirements, which cut into the low-cost labor model many operate on [S3].
